answer.label: Not Max Planck — an 1890s translation credited to “Müller”
answer.sourceLine: The line is the English gloss of a German couplet, “Nichts ist dem Menschen so schwer zu tragen, / Als eine Reihe von guten Tagen,” printed in James Wood’s Dictionary of Quotations (London: Warne, 1893) and credited there simply to “Müller.” Wikiquote lists it as misattributed to Planck and names Max Müller as the source; nobody has tied it to anything Planck wrote.

source.heading: Where the line really appears

docMeta.dd: Dictionary of Quotations from Ancient and Modern, English and Foreign Sources
London: Frederick Warne and Co., 1893 (Project Gutenberg transcription); Wikiquote cites the 1899 edition

source.excerpt: Nichts ist dem Menschen so schwer zu tragen, / Als eine Reihe von guten Tagen — No burden is so heavy for a man to bear as a succession of happy days. Müller.
trail: Wikiquote’s Max Planck page lists this line under Misattributed, crediting Max Müller, as quoted in James Wood’s Dictionary of Quotations (1899) ↗.

The Project Gutenberg transcription of Wood’s dictionary ↗, made from the 1893 London edition, already has the exact English wording. It translates the German couplet “Nichts ist dem Menschen so schwer zu tragen, / Als eine Reihe von guten Tagen” and credits it to “Müller.”
The Internet Archive holds a scan of the 1899 Warne edition ↗, the edition Wikiquote cites.
The couplet closely echoes a rhyme by Goethe in his Sprichwörtliches: “Alles in der Welt läßt sich ertragen, / Nur nicht eine Reihe von schönen Tagen” (text at Projekt Gutenberg ↗).
source.excerptNote: As printed among the German entries in Wood’s 1893 edition: the German couplet comes first, then Wood’s English rendering, then the credit. Wood does not say which Müller he meant.

author.name: Max Müller
author.heading: About the credited author
author.bio: Friedrich Max Müller was a German-born British comparative philologist and Orientalist, and one of the founders of Indology and religious studies as Western academic fields. He directed the Sacred Books of the East, a 50-volume series of English translations. Wood’s 1893 dictionary credits this couplet only to “Müller”; the identification with Max Müller comes from Wikiquote.

misattribution.heading: Who gets the credit, and why
misattribution.intro: Quote sites widely credit this line to the physicist Max Planck, but no work of his is ever cited for it. The English wording was already in print in 1893, credited to a “Müller.”

items.why: Wikiquote ↗ lists the line under Planck’s Misattributed heading and credits it to Max Müller instead. No source has been found showing where the Planck version started. One possibility is a mix-up between two famous Germans named Max, but that is our guess, and no source documents it.
Wood’s 1893 dictionary ↗ credits the German couplet only to “Müller.” Wikiquote reads that name as the philologist Friedrich Max Müller. Wood himself never gives a first name.

Goethe’s couplet “Alles in der Welt läßt sich ertragen, / Nur nicht eine Reihe von schönen Tagen” (Sprichwörtliches ↗) has the same rhyme and the same idea, but it is a different German text from the one Wood translated.

misattribution.truthLine: The documented source is Wood’s Dictionary of Quotations, which already has this exact English wording in its 1893 edition ↗, credited to “Müller” and not to Planck.

context.heading: An old German idea about too much good luck
lead: The idea that unbroken good fortune is harder to bear than hardship was a familiar one in German verse. Goethe put it in a rhyme: “Alles in der Welt läßt sich ertragen, / Nur nicht eine Reihe von schönen Tagen.” The couplet in Wood’s dictionary, “Nichts ist dem Menschen so schwer zu tragen, / Als eine Reihe von guten Tagen,” uses the same rhyme and the same thought in different words.

The English line now passed around under Max Planck’s name is Wood’s own translation of that couplet. It sat in a Victorian reference book, credited to “Müller,” long before anyone attached it to the physicist.

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote's Max Planck page lists 'No burden is so heavy for a man to bear as a succession of happy days' under Misattributed and credits it to Max Müller, as quoted in James Wood's Dictionary of Quotations (1899).

Wood's Dictionary of Quotations (title page: London, Frederick Warne and Co., 1893) prints the German couplet 'Nichts ist dem Menschen so schwer zu tragen, / Als eine Reihe von guten Tagen' with the English 'No burden is so heavy for a man to bear as a succession of happy days', credited to 'Müller'.
The Internet Archive item dictionaryquota00woodgoog is the 1899 London/New York F. Warne and Co. edition of Wood's Dictionary of Quotations.
Goethe's Sprichwörtliches, as printed in Goethes Reimsprüche, contains the couplet 'Alles in der Welt läßt sich ertragen, / Nur nicht eine Reihe von schönen Tagen.'
Friedrich Max Müller (1823–1900) was a German-born British comparative philologist and Orientalist who directed the Sacred Books of the East.
Max Planck (1858–1947) was a German theoretical physicist and the originator of quantum theory.
